extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. To succeed on LAMBADA, computational models cannot simply rely on local context, but must be able to keep track of information in the broader discourse.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández; CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam
extraction.citeAs: Paperno, D., Kruszewski, G., Lazaridou, A., Pham, Q. N., Bernardi, R., Pezzelle, S., Baroni, M., Boleda, G., & Fernández, R. (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (pp. 1525–1534). Berlin, Germany.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were sourced from the BookCorpus (unpublished novels). After duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material, the corpus contained 5,325 novels and 465 million words. Novels were randomly divided into training and development+testing partitions. Passages from the dev+test partition were filtered using language models to remove easy-to-predict items, then evaluated by human subjects via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing in a three-step process to ensure target words were guessable only with broad context.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The BookCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015), containing unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Passages were filtered using a combination of four language models (a pre-trained RNN and three models trained on the BookCorpus: a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded. The remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects in a three-step crowdsourcing pipeline: (1) one subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; (2) if correct, a second subject also guessed from the whole passage; (3) if also correct, additional subjects tried to guess from the target sentence only (up to 10 unsuccessful guesses or 3 guesses per subject). Only passages passing all three steps were included.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list were applied to the BookCorpus. Novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Context size was set as the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. Passages where the target word had probability ≥0.00175 under any of four language models were excluded. Vocabulary was restricted to the 60K most frequent words in the training set.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects annotated passages via CrowdFlower in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word given the whole passage (context + target sentence); if correct, (2) a second subject guessed the target word given the whole passage; if also correct, (3) additional subjects tried to guess the target word given only the target sentence, with up to 3 guesses per subject and up to 10 unsuccessful guesses total. Passages were included in LAMBADA only if steps 1 and 2 were passed (two consecutive subjects correctly guessed the word from the whole passage) and step 3 was failed (no subject guessed the word from the sentence alone). The same subject was not allowed to judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: 84–86% of items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2, and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all selection steps. The strict hit-or-miss approach required exact word matches; synonymous or plausible alternatives were not accepted due to practical and methodological challenges in determining substitutability at scale.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 subjects for broad-context guessing (steps 1 and 2), and up to 10 subjects for sentence-only guessing (step 3, with 3 guesses per subject).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models used for automated filtering: a pre-trained RNN (Mikolov et al., 2011), a standard 4-gram model trained on BookCorpus, an RNN trained on BookCorpus, and a feed-forward model trained on BookCorpus.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus are available for download at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/. The test set was to be made available at the time of a planned public competition. No further versioning or deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: LAMBADA is intended to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text, promoting progress in language understanding research.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA (48% of target words), while verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are underrepresented compared to the input data distribution. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. LAMBADA items contain quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% vs. 61%). The dataset is sourced exclusively from unpublished novels in English, limiting genre and language diversity.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: LAMBADA was designed to challenge language models with harder-than-average examples where broad context understanding is crucial; standard language models are bound to fail on it by design since one of the first filters was to choose passages where simple language models failed to predict the upcoming word. The dataset is limited to English narrative text from unpublished novels. The strict exact-match criterion for annotation may exclude valid synonymous answers. Cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve filtering quality.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing/evaluation of language models and computational models for text understanding, specifically for broad discourse context understanding. The development set can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of LAMBADA passages. Models should be trained on raw text (the provided training corpus of 2,662 novels) following standard unsupervised language modeling practice, not trained specifically on LAMBADA-style passages.
